**Paris prosecutors opened an investigation on 7 Nov into whether foreign powers sent the hoax bomb threats** that hit European flights from 2 to 6 Nov; no new flight threat had been reported by Sunday. [15]

**Bulgarian prosecutors said on 7 Nov that human remains were found on a drone-hit tanker towed to Varna;** Reuters counts at least nine cargo ships hit off Romania and Bulgaria in October, about 34 sailors dead or missing, and France has extended its Atlantique 2 patrol from Romania. [16, 17]

**Koalicja 26.2, the first Multinational Force–Ukraine exercise, opens in Poland on 9 Nov** with 2,800 troops from 11 nations and no US forces, the day before US–Russia–Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi. [10, 18, 19]

items.h: Russia fires 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv region as Moscow names its Abu Dhabi team
items.body: The Air Force said Russia launched 172 drones and Iskander-M, Zircon, KN-23 and S-400 missiles overnight into 7 Nov, mainly at Kyiv region; President Zelensky: “Russia used 36 missiles approaching their targets along a ballistic trajectory. Only four missiles were taken down.” [11, 12] Substations linking the Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear plants to central Ukraine were hit and six people were injured in Kyiv. [13, 23] Overnight into 8 Nov the Air Force counted 164 drones and three Kh-59/69 missiles, with 137 drones shot down or suppressed and hits at 23 locations; Rostov region's governor said a drone damaged a bridge on the highway from Rostov-on-Don to occupied Ukraine. [14, 24] Kyiv Independent reported that Vladimir Medinsky leads Russia's delegation with deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, GRU chief Igor Kostyukov and Yury Zhigarlovsky of the General Staff. [19]
items.next: Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 Nov [19]; the Ukraine Defense Contact Group meets in mid-November, date not given. [25]

items.h: Iran's Guards say two tankers hit mines as a strike near Sanaa kills 33
items.body: The Revolutionary Guards navy said late on 7 Nov that two tankers were burning after hitting mines, saying they had “switched off their navigation and positioning systems” and used an “unauthorized route”; no ship was named, and Iranian agencies reported explosions on Qeshm and at Jask, Sirik and Bandar Abbas without a cause. [26, 27] Guards spokesman Gen. Hossein Mohebbi said of Iran's self-imposed missile-range limit: “That restriction has been lifted for us.” [28] On 8 Nov the UAE coast guard evacuated all 22 crew from a burning, unnamed cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman. [29] In Gaza the health ministry counts 1,610 killed since the October 2025 ceasefire, and the first winter storm flooded about 70,000 tents. [30, 31] In Yemen a strike the Houthis blame on Saudi Arabia killed 33 people at al-Shariya near Sanaa; on 8 Nov coalition spokesman Col. Turki al-Maliki said Saudi air defences intercepted “three Houthi ballistic missiles, two cruise missiles and one drone”, most of them aimed at Riyadh. [32, 33, 34]
items.next: G7 foreign ministers meet in Paris on 9–10 Nov [35]; Lloyd's List publishes its next Hormuz brief on 19 Nov. [36]

items.h: Norway detains a falsely flagged Chinese heavy-lift ship near Andøya air base
items.body: The Norwegian Coastal Administration detained the Ya Qing Hai Yang, sanctioned by the EU and US over Arctic LNG 2 deliveries, after it sailed the Northern Sea Route from Zhuhai; Arve Dimmen: “the vessel was flying a false flag and lacked the correct certificates. The vessel has been detained.” It lies in the Andfjord near Andøya, where the Svalbard cables land. [37, 38] Greenland's parliament ratified the US–Denmark–Greenland defence agreement on 3 Nov; Foreign Minister Mute Egede: “We must accept that peace and stability are no longer something we can take for granted.” [39] Norway is placing NASAMS sensors with the border battalion at Kirkenes to detect stray drones, and the new US ambassador visited the Russian border on 6 Nov. [40, 41]
items.next: The Folketing holds its first reading of the Greenland agreement on 11 Nov and votes on 19 Nov. [39]

items.h: Taiwan takes its second F-16V batch as PLA sorties fall to four
items.body: Taiwan's defence ministry counted four Chinese military aircraft sorties, two of them in the south-western air defence identification zone, six navy ships and two official ships in the 24 hours to 06:00 on 8 Nov, against 11 sorties a day earlier. [42, 43] Three F-16V Block 70s landed at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung on 8 Nov, bringing deliveries to five of 66. [44] Beijing said it “is in communication with relevant parties” on a Xi–Trump–Putin meeting at APEC in Shenzhen. [45] In Beijing on 6 Nov Workers' Party secretary Kim Song-nam met Politburo Standing Committee member Cai Qi, his third high-level meeting of the visit. [46]
items.next: APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen on 18–19 Nov; Taiwan holds local elections on 28 Nov.

items.h: Human remains found on a drone-hit tanker in Varna; France extends its Black Sea patrol
items.body: Bulgaria's prosecution service said on 7 Nov that “badly damaged human remains were discovered” during debris clearing on a San Marino-flagged ship hit by a drone off Romania in October and towed to a Varna yard; AFP identifies it as the Wine Trader, seven of whose 12 crew were missing. [16, 47] Reuters counts at least nine cargo ships hit near the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts in October, with about 34 sailors dead or missing. [17] A French Atlantique 2 at Mihail Kogălniceanu since 18 Oct had its mission extended past 6 Nov; its commander: “We are able to detect. We are not able to neutralise and intercept these kind of drones.” [17] On 5 Nov Moldova announced a five-year exit ban on Transnistrian leader Vadim Krasnoselsky after President Putin decorated him in the Kremlin on 4 Nov. [48, 49]
items.next: The Atlantique 2 stays “for a few weeks” from 5 Nov [17]; Transnistria's unrecognised leadership vote is due in December, date not set. [48]

feature.title: Red Sea and Yemen, November to November: transits down a quarter, the coast in Houthi hands
body: In November 2025 the Houthis were not attacking ships, and PortWatch counted 1,133 transits of the Bab el-Mandeb in the month, against 2,438 in October 2023. [50, 51] On 15 January Maersk's MECL service went back through Suez; it suspended the route in March and restored it on 9 July. [52]

After the US and Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February, two Houthi officials told AP the group would resume attacks on shipping, but the Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) reported on 31 March: “No verified Houthi attacks against commercial vessels have been confirmed since the escalation of hostilities on 28 February.” [51, 53] Saudi crude moved west instead: Kpler put exports from Yanbu through the strait at 3.5 million barrels a day in June, and monthly tanker transits rose from 384 in November to 464 in March. [54, 50]

July broke the pattern. After the 13 July strike on Sanaa airport the Houthis fired at Abha, and on 20 July they declared that “all vessels loading or discharging cargo at or from any Saudi ports are prohibited.” [55, 54] Transits fell from 1,043 in July to 848 in August and 797 in September. [50] On 11 August missiles hit the Egyptian-owned Tihamah and killed at least six, the first shipping deaths linked to the Houthis since 28 February. [56]

On 10–11 September Houthi forces took Mocha, Dhubab and Perim Island; spokesman Yahya Saree said: “Maritime navigation is safe for all companies except Saudi ships, which have already been banned.” [57, 58] Saudi-backed forces counter-attacked on 4 October, and on 10 October a missile hit Riyadh's King Khalid airport, killing 12 by the Saudi aviation authority's count. [59] On 2 November Houthi forces were within 80 km of Aden. [60] October's 864 transits were 64.6% below October 2023 and 23.7% below November 2025. [50]
timeline: A Houthi court in Sanaa sentences 17 people to death for spying for the US, Israel and Saudi Arabia. [61]
Saudi Arabia strikes a weapons shipment at Mukalla; Riyadh says the two vessels had switched off tracking. The UAE announces it will withdraw its remaining troops. [62]
Maersk's MECL service returns to the Suez route. [52]
After US and Israeli strikes on Iran, two Houthi officials say attacks on shipping and Israel will resume. [51]
The Houthis fire missiles at southern Israel, their first attack on Israel since the Iran war began. [63]
JMIC: no verified Houthi attack on merchant ships since 28 Feb; GNSS interference persists in the Gulf of Aden. [53]
Maersk restores MECL trans-Suez sailings, suspended in March. [52]
Yemen's government strikes Sanaa airport; the Houthis fire missiles and drones at Abha and warn airlines off Saudi airspace. [55]
The Houthis declare a blockade of ships loading or discharging at Saudi ports. [54]
Saudi Arabia announces a Multinational Maritime Defence Alliance of 14 countries in Riyadh. [64]
Three Houthi ballistic missiles hit the cargo ship Tihamah; at least six killed. [56]
Houthi forces take Mocha, about 75 km north of the strait. [57]
The Houthis take Perim Island and Dhubab and hold Yemen's whole Red Sea coast. [58, 65]
A missile hits Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport: 12 killed, 309 wounded. [59]
Houthi forces are within 80 km of Aden; Saudi strikes hit Ras Issa port. [60]
after: Monthly figures are sums of PortWatch's daily estimates, which PortWatch may revise; the government's 8 Oct claim to have cleared Perim is disputed by the Houthis, and no source confirms who holds the island now. [50, 59]

incidents.text: Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said hackers published personal data on him and his family on the darknet and offered to pay for more; Prime Minister Meloni's office expressed solidarity over “the activities of pro-Russian hackers”. [66]

incidents.text: Varna prosecutors said on 7 Nov that human remains were found on the drone-struck tanker Wine Trader in a Bulgarian repair yard; seven of its 12 crew had been missing, and AFP counts at least nine merchant ships hit by drones off Romania and Bulgaria since early October, with 34 dead or missing. [47]

Posts claimed Chancellor Merz called the Hamburg Nord Stream trial senseless because “Das deutsche Volk hat der Ukraine verziehen”, the German people have forgiven Ukraine; no record exists and the government called it “Desinformation”. [68]

leads.title: Paris opens a probe into foreign links behind the airliner hoax wave
leads.teaser: No new flight threat surfaced on Saturday; the wave of 2–6 Nov now has a prosecutor asking who sent it and for whom.
rows: The Paris prosecutor's office said on 7 Nov it is investigating to find “the authors of the emails who disseminated this false information... and to determine any potential links they may have to foreign powers”. [15]

Some emails were signed “fighters of the Male State”, a Russian movement banned in Russia since 2021 whose founder denies involvement; the newsroom emails of 6 Nov were signed “Mikhail Andropov”. [15, 69]

A0 to A1. The Independent, citing the Financial Times, reports that European intelligence services point to pro-Kremlin activists or hacking groups, with the role of Russian state services unclear. [69] EU Transport Commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas activated EU aviation-security information sharing on 6 Nov and said it was “too early” to link the hoaxes. [70]
The Czech man arrested at Schiphol on 5 Nov for a spoken threat at a gate was released on 6 Nov; prosecution is undecided. [71]

More than 50 leaders meet at the European Political Community summit in Dublin on 12 Nov under Ireland's largest security operation; Taoiseach Micheál Martin: “We're confident that will go off safely.” [72]
leads.sw: A criminal probe into foreign links is the first step toward the attribution NATO needs before calling the wave hybrid aggression; until then the J9 tracks it against baseline requirement 7 (civil transportation) as a host-nation police matter.

leads.title: German intelligence joins the cold-chain probe as the method reaches medicine
leads.teaser: The domestic intelligence service says the refrigeration attacks are under intelligence investigation; Berlin still names no actor.
rows: The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) told Handelsblatt on 6 Nov the incidents “are the subject of current intelligence investigations”, and the joint centre against hybrid threats of the BfV, BND, MAD and police is on the case. [73, 74]
Automated scans, outdated software and default passwords, in one case entry through an outside maintenance firm; units were switched to defrost or heating, up to 50 °C. [74]
Correctiv reported on 5 Nov, citing the federal cyber agency, that a German pharmaceutical distributor's medicine-cooling systems were also attacked. [75]

A0. The interior ministry: “keine Erkenntnisse ..., die eine eindeutige Zuordnung dieser Angriffe zu einem spezifischen Akteur oder einer staatlichen Stelle zulassen würden”, no findings that allow attribution to an actor or state body. Peskov called the accusations “absurd”. [73, 75]
leads.sw: Medicine cooling moves the campaign from baseline requirement 4 (food and water) to 5 (mass casualties): ask which host-nation pharmacy and blood-bank contractors in the Joint Operations Area use remote-managed controllers with default passwords.

pattern: **From hoax to case file:** Paris now investigates the airliner emails for foreign links, and the newsroom threats carried a second signature. [15, 69]
**The same weak point, a wider target set:** default passwords and maintenance access opened supermarket fridges and, by one report, a medicine distributor's cooling. [74, 75]
**Personal pressure on ministers:** Italy's foreign minister says his family's data were leaked, and Rome blames pro-Russian hackers. [66]
**Drones in NATO waters:** nine merchant ships hit off Romania and Bulgaria since early October, 34 dead or missing. [47]

europe.h: A gunman kills six on Kraków's Main Market Square; Tusk calls it an attack
europe.body: A gunman firing from a car on the Rynek Główny at about 15:00 on 7 Nov killed four women and two men, one of them British, and wounded 15, 12 critically; three more bodies were found at his home. [22] The suspect, a Pole in his mid-twenties with a gun licence, used a civilian AR-15; Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said he was fascinated by far-right ideology, and authorities treat him as a lone actor. [22] Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it a “grauenvolles Attentat”, a horrific attack, in tagesschau's German rendering; Slovakia's Robert Fico said his country “stands firmly” with Poland. [22, 76]
europe.sw: Mourning runs to Monday and Independence Day marches follow on 11 Nov: watch whether Polish authorities raise the alert level, a baseline requirement 5 (mass casualties) question in a frontline ally.

europe.h: A US text on a “new European security architecture” goes to the Abu Dhabi talks
europe.body: RTBF reported on 7 Nov that a 423-word text by Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff proposes a “nouvelle architecture de sécurité européenne”, calls NATO “central” and refers to “competing security concerns” between Europe and Russia; Politico, cited by RTBF, says three NATO diplomats were not told in advance. [77] EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas in Warsaw on 6 Nov: “Poutine n'a pas de droit de veto sur la sécurité européenne”, Putin has no veto over European security. [77]
europe.sw: A US–Russian text on Europe's security order, drafted without the allies, would bear directly on the posture and force-sharing assumptions in JFC Brunssum's regional plans.

europe.h: De Wever gets ten more days as the coalition pledges to restart budget talks
europe.body: RTBF wrote on 7 Nov that the Prime Minister “a donc obtenu un sursis de 10 jours”, won a ten-day reprieve, with bilateral talks from Mon 9 Nov. [78] Belgian 10-year rates stand at 4.4% against Germany's 3.4%, and debt at 110.2% of GDP. [79]
europe.sw: NATO's and SHAPE's host stays on provisional twelfths until 16 Nov at the earliest, holding Belgian defence commitments at this year's level.

countries.h: Magyar takes four ministers to Berlin on Tuesday for defence, energy and Ukraine
countries.body: Prime Minister Péter Magyar meets Chancellor Merz at 11:00 on Tue 10 Nov with Foreign Minister Anita Orbán, Economy and Energy Minister István Kapitány, Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi and Interior Minister Gábor Pósfai; the German side lists “European affairs, defense, economic cooperation, and continued support for Ukraine”, with a press conference at 13:30. [80, 81] Croatia's Adria crude line, MOL's alternative to Druzhba, was damaged during works on 6 Nov and the leak stopped. [82]
countries.sw: Baseline requirement 2 (energy): Hungary's crude rests on Druzhba and Adria, and a Berlin visit with energy and defence ministers is where diversification money and German industrial ties get traded.

q.t: A kormányfőt négy minisztere, köztük Orbán Anita külügyminiszter és Kapitány István gazdasági miniszter is elkíséri.
q.en: The head of government will be accompanied by four of his ministers, among them Foreign Minister Anita Orbán and Economy Minister István Kapitány.

countries.h: Hungary will fly Baltic Air Policing again in 2028 while holding Ukraine's clusters
countries.body: Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said in a video on 7 Nov that Hungary will take part in Baltic Air Policing in 2028, its fifth rotation: “Nagyon örülünk és büszkék vagyunk arra, hogy közreműködünk a balti légtér védelmében és biztosításában”, we are very glad and proud to help defend and secure Baltic airspace. Its last rotation, from 1 Aug 2025, put four JAS-39 Gripens and about 80 personnel at Šiauliai. [83, 84] Világgazdaság reports Hungary again withheld approval for Ukraine's EU clusters 4 and 5 on 3 Nov. [85]
countries.sw: A Tisza government that commits fighters to the Baltics while slowing Ukraine's EU path separates its NATO contribution from its Ukraine policy: track both in the profile.

q.t: Magyarország 2028-ban ötödik alkalommal vállal szerepet a Balti Légtérrendészeti Misszióban…
q.en: In 2028 Hungary takes part in the Baltic Air Policing Mission for the fifth time…

countries.h: Fico calls Slovakia's EU accession referendum of 2003 rigged before Tuesday's votes
countries.body: Speaking with former Czech president Václav Klaus on 6 Nov, Prime Minister Robert Fico said the referendum of 2003 on joining the EU was falsified; MP Tomáš Taraba: “ako ďaleko sme od tvrdení, že sú sfalšované aj voľby”, how far are we from claiming elections are falsified too. [86] Fico ruled out early elections and said he expects some bills to fail when parliament votes on Tue 10 Nov at 11:00, the coalition's first test with 75 secure votes. [87]
countries.sw: Baseline requirement 1 (continuity of government): a coalition one vote short of a majority now passes or loses bills case by case, which slows any defence or civil-preparedness law.

q.t: Premiér tvrdí, že keby referendum nebolo sfalšované, nebolo by úspešné.
q.en: The prime minister claims that if the referendum had not been falsified, it would not have succeeded.

countries.h: Germany's LÜKEX 2026 tests 180 bodies against drought, heat and disinformation
countries.body: The Federal Office of Civil Protection (BBK) and the interior ministry ran a desk exercise from 4 to 6 Nov with about 180 federal and state authorities, aid organisations and infrastructure operators on a scenario of multi-year drought and weeks at 40–45 °C, with injected IT and power failures, water shortages, hospital bottlenecks and disinformation. [88, 89] BBK President Grit Tüngler: “Die diesjährige LÜKEX mit dem Schwerpunkt Dürre und Hitzewelle ist ein wichtiger Schritt in diese Richtung.” The evaluation takes about a year. [88]
countries.sw: One exercise touched four baseline requirements (energy, food and water, mass casualties, civil communications); the evaluation is the German reference the J9 can ask the BBK liaison for in 2027.

q.t: Von Mittwoch bis Freitag testen fast 180 Organisationen mit der nationalen Übung LÜKEX26 ihr Krisenmanagement, wie das Bundesamt am Montag in Bonn erklärte.
q.en: From Wednesday to Friday almost 180 organisations are testing their crisis management in the national exercise LÜKEX26, the federal office said in Bonn on Monday.

countries.h: CDU and CSU leaders reject Pistorius's view that conscription is not needed
countries.body: Defence Minister Boris Pistorius told the Funke papers on 7 Nov that he sees no need to return to conscription for now: the ministry counts about 38,500 applications this year, 24% more than a year earlier, and troop strength passed 190,000 in early October. [90] Defence Committee chair Thomas Röwekamp (CDU): “Wenn die Freiwilligkeit dafür nicht ausreicht, müssen wir zur Wehrpflicht zurückkehren”, if volunteering is not enough we must return to conscription; CSU leader Markus Söder: “Wir brauchen wieder eine echte Wehrpflicht.” [91, 92] Pistorius presents a study of unreported sexual misconduct in the Bundeswehr next week. [90]
countries.sw: The coalition's split on conscription decides whether Germany reaches the 260,000 active troops it wants by 2035, the manpower behind its host-nation and reinforcement roles. [90]

q.t: Wenn die Freiwilligkeit dafür nicht ausreicht, müssen wir zur Wehrpflicht zurückkehren.
q.en: If volunteering is not enough for that, we must return to conscription.

euregio.h: Landgraaf's Megaland asylum site takes its first 40 residents on Monday
euregio.body: The emergency site on the Pinkpop grounds, about 5 km from Heerlen, houses up to 280 people from 35 countries, four to an 18 m² unit, with a GP and a classroom; residents must be on site from 22:00 to 07:00. It runs to May 2027, closes for Pinkpop and reopens from September 2027 to May 2028. Several hundred people toured it on Saturday and dozens protested, without incident. [93]
euregio.fy: Expect more police and COA traffic around Megaland from Monday; nothing changes for Pinkpop dates.

euregio.h: The trial over the explosive and planned knife attack on an ICE opens in Aachen on Tuesday
euregio.body: A 20-year-old German charged with attempted murder goes on trial at Aachen Regional Court on Tue 10 Nov, with eight hearing days to mid-December; he allegedly set off two softair grenades on an ICE near Siegburg on 2 Apr as a diversion for a knife attack announced in a manifesto, and ten people were lightly injured. [94]
euregio.fy: Expect security checks around the Landgericht in Aachen on hearing days.

items.h: Koalicja 26.2 opens Monday: 2,800 troops from 11 nations train for postwar Ukraine
items.body: The first exercise of the Multinational Force–Ukraine runs in Poland from 9 to 22 Nov with troops from Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, Türkiye and the UK; Britain sends 300 from 7 Brigade, Typhoons and a Voyager tanker, and Türkiye stands up the maritime element in Istanbul. [10] It is not under NATO command, US troops are not taking part, and the Polish ministry speaks of nearly 2,000 Polish soldiers “in addition to the foreign forces”. [18] The force headquarters is due to move from Paris to London this year. [10]
items.sw: Dutch, Belgian and German units train for a mission outside NATO command: their availability for JFC Brunssum's regional plans while they are earmarked for Ukraine is the force-generation question to raise.

items.h: Denmark and Lithuania buy Finland's Blocker sea mines through a five-nation scheme
items.body: Defense News reported on 6 Nov that Denmark and Lithuania are buying Forcit's Blocker mines through the Finnish-led Naval Mines Cooperation with Germany and Norway; Finland signed the contract in June, worth “hundreds of millions of Euros”, and Germany may announce a purchase this year. [95]
items.sw: Shared mine stocks in the Baltic approaches are deterrence by denial at the sea end of JFC Brunssum's area, bought jointly to shorten delivery.

items.h: Resolute Reforger ends in eastern Latvia after two weeks with 14 nations
items.body: The exercise of the Canadian-led Multinational Brigade Latvia, about 3,000 soldiers and 1,000 pieces of equipment, ends on 8 Nov with return movements on Latvian roads since 4 Nov; no closing statement has been published. [96]

items.h: Shield AI agrees to buy counter-drone radar maker Echodyne for $5.3 billion
items.body: Shield AI announced on 5 Nov that it will acquire Echodyne, whose solid-state radars track more than 1,000 objects at once and which won a $250 million, 36-month counter-drone contract from Joint Interagency Task Force 401 in September; chief executive Gary Steele will split the company into autonomy software, autonomous systems and mission systems. No closing date was given. [97]
items.sw: Radar plus autonomy in one firm shortens the sensor-to-interceptor chain that base defence in Europe now buys piecemeal.

items.h: Rheinmetall cuts its 2026 sales guidance to about €13.2 billion as its backlog hits €78 billion
items.body: Rheinmetall's third-quarter statement of 5 Nov gives nine-month sales of €8,376 million, up 38%, a backlog of €78.0 billion against €56.7 billion a year earlier, and lowers 2026 guidance to about €13.2 billion on delays to the Arminius vehicle and artillery-ammunition testing. Weapon and ammunition sales rose 34% to €2,705 million, helped by a Hungarian package and rounds for Ukraine; an artillery plant is going up in Lithuania. [98]
items.sw: A record backlog with slipping deliveries means Europe's 155 mm ramp-up is limited by test and plant capacity, not orders; the Lithuanian plant sits inside JFC Brunssum's area.

items.h: Kyiv says Russia flies drones over its own Rassvet satellite constellation

research.title: Anticipating Allies' Responses to U.S. Retrenchment from Europe: How France, Germany, Poland, and the United Kingdom Might Adapt to Alternative U.S. Approaches
research.authors: Miranda Priebe, Stephanie Pezard, Anna M. Dowd, James Black, Paul van Hooft, Clara de Lataillade, Zachary Burdette, Daniel Cebul, Nathaniel Edenfield and Scott Behmer
summary: The report studies “limited U.S. retrenchment—reductions in, but not elimination of, U.S. defense commitments and military posture”, and asks how four allies would answer it, alongside further tariffs and a change in US policy toward Russia. Its topline: “As U.S. retrenchment from Europe gets underway, allies' reactions will hinge on the manner in which Washington pulls back.” Because all four see Russia as a high threat, the authors expect broadly similar responses. [115]

The central finding contrasts two paths: “A coordinated, gradual drawdown would likely lead allies to preserve security ties with Washington; a sudden, large-scale withdrawal could cause allies to accelerate efforts to reduce dependence on U.S. arms.” Using posture to reward or punish single allies “might create fissures that undermine regional cooperation”, and a US détente with Russia that does not put European security first could lead allies to curtail intelligence-sharing. The authors find that “None of the four allies will pursue security alignment with Russia or China, regardless of the U.S. approach to retrenchment,” and that France and the UK “will struggle to meet defense spending targets”. On the posture review they write: “As of October 2026, it is not clear whether the U.S. Department of War has a Europe posture review that will produce such a plan or only decisions about immediate changes in U.S. regional presence.” They recommend that Washington share long-term drawdown plans so allies can phase investment, “Because no one ally is prepared to fill the U.S. role”. [115]
findings: **Footprint:** “around 80,000 service members stationed in Europe across roughly 30 bases”; assigned troops numbered 67,000–69,000 in 2022–25. [115]

**Posture as leverage:** in May 2026 the department “abruptly canceled the rotational deployment of roughly 4,000 soldiers to Poland”, then the President pledged 5,000 troops at an undefined later date. [115]
**Poland:** defence spending rose from 1.88% of GDP in 2014 to 4.12% in 2024 and heads for 5% in 2026; the force grew from 99,000 in 2010 to an estimated 216,000. [115]

**Germany and France:** a €649 billion five-year plan takes Germany from 2.4% of GDP in 2025 to 3.5% by 2029; France's debt averaged 112% of GDP over 2020–24, its “Achilles' heel” in one interviewee's words. [115]

research.method: Three strands: lessons from RAND's Cold War retrenchment cases and the international-relations literature; official documents and public debate in each country in 2025–26; and 51 anonymous interviews (France 18, Germany 10, Poland 14, UK 9), mostly April–November 2025, over a one-to-five-year horizon. The authors concede the findings “do not necessarily apply to all NATO allies”, that the interviews preceded the Iran war, and that “We did not objectively assess allies' ability to replace U.S. capabilities”. [115]
research.sw: For Brunssum: the report's distinction between a phased and a sudden drawdown is the planning variable for the Joint Force Command's host-nation-support and reinforcement arrangements, which assume US enablers on the ground; ask which of our plans would survive a short-notice cancellation like Poland's in May.

research.title: Across the Globe, People Increasingly Say Social Media Is Harming Democracy
research.authors: Richard Wike, Maria Smerkovich and Moira Fagan
summary: Pew's Spring 2026 Global Attitudes Survey finds that “the view that social media is harming democracy has become more common”, rising significantly since 2022 or 2023 in most countries with trend data. The world still leans positive: “a median of 55% think social media has had a positive impact on democracy, while a median of 35% say it has had a negative one.” Wealth sorts the answers, and Europe splits: “Poles, Italians and Greeks tend to see social media's impact positively, while majorities in the U.K., Germany, France and the Netherlands say it has been bad for democracy.” People hold both views at once: medians of 79% say it makes it easier to manipulate people with false information and 68% that it divides them, while 77% say it informs them. [116]
findings: The Netherlands is the most negative of 37 countries: 70% say social media is bad for democracy, up from 54% in 2022. [116]
Germany shows Europe's largest swing, from 41% “bad” in 2022 to 61% in 2026; “made people more divided” rose there from 65% to 82%. [116]
In Hungary “bad” rose from 22% to 42% and in Poland from 15% to 35%, though both changed survey method in 2024. [116]
In the UK, 60% of 18–34s say social media's influence on democracy has been good, against 31% of those aged 50 and over. [116]
research.method: 45,658 adults in 37 countries: 42,151 in 36 countries interviewed 8 Feb – 13 May 2026 by telephone, face to face and online, plus 3,507 on Pew's American Trends Panel. It measures what people believe social media does, not its effect, and Pew cautions on the Hungarian and Polish trends after their switch from face-to-face to telephone interviews. [116]
research.sw: Public belief that information is easy to manipulate is the ground any influence campaign works on, and it is highest in the host nation.

research.title: CTRL + ALT + Europe? Most Europeans support homegrown digital alternatives. The European digital sovereignty debate hasn't yet fully matched that ambition.
summary: A representative eupinions survey of June 2026 finds that “digital sovereignty” is familiar in Brussels but not to most citizens: only 49% know the term, yet 72% “want Europe to have control over key digital technologies and infrastructure”, and 73% “are concerned that critical European services could be remotely disabled by actors outside Europe – the so-called kill switch scenario.” Support is strongest in the political centre and falls sharply on the far right. The authors argue Europe should not “replicate the centralized, proprietary hyperscaler paradigm”, and that its advantage lies in “decentralized infrastructures whose resilience derives from not having a single point of failure.” [117]
findings: 73% across the EU fear a remote kill switch, 35% “very concerned”; 82% in Portugal, 79% in the Netherlands, 77% in Germany, 59% in Romania. [117]
83% want critical public systems to be transparent and secure, 78% want legal redress in Europe and 69% want data stored and processed in Europe. [117]
67% would switch to European AI, social-media and cloud services if they worked as well; only 43% think Europe regulates non-European digital services successfully. [117]
The Netherlands has the highest familiarity with the term, 62%; Germany and Poland the lowest, 42% each. [117]
research.method: Online eupinions panel in all 27 member states, June 2026, 16,795 respondents aged 18–69, weighted to Eurostat, effective margin of error ±1.0 point for EU-wide figures; country figures only for the ten largest samples. All items are stated preferences, people over 69 are excluded, and on the far-right pattern the authors write: “The survey cannot establish the reasons behind this pattern.” [117]
research.sw: A remote kill switch on cloud and communications services is baseline requirement 6 (civil communications) stated in public-opinion terms, and three Europeans in four already fear it.

philosophy.where: Book I, Chapter 1, §24: “War is a mere continuation of policy by other means”
philosophy.quote: We see, therefore, that war is not merely a political act, but also a real political instrument, a continuation of political commerce, a carrying out of the same by other means. All beyond this which is strictly peculiar to war relates merely to the peculiar nature of the means which it uses. That the tendencies and views of policy shall not be incompatible with these means, the art of war in general and the commander in each particular case may demand, and this claim is truly not a trifling one. But however powerfully this may react on political views in particular cases, still it must always be regarded as only a modification of them; for the political view is the object, war is the means, and the means must always include the object in our conception.
philosophy.translation: J. J. Graham, London, 1873 (“political commerce” renders politischer Verkehr, political dealings)
philosophy.gloss: The passage closes the argument of the first chapter: war in pure conception tends to the extreme and would displace policy, but real war is “a pulsation of violent force” that lasts long enough to stay under “the will of a guiding intelligence”, so it remains an instrument. [118] What is peculiar to war is only its means, and the soldier may fairly demand that policy not ask the impossible of them, but that demand modifies policy and never replaces it. The point carries weight because Clausewitz called this chapter the only finished part of the book, and §27 draws the consequence: the first act of judgement is to understand what kind of war one is in. [118] The strongest objections attack the premise that war has a definable object: Simone Weil argued in 1936, against Clausewitz, that wars are absurd because “they are conflicts with no definable objective” [119], and John Keegan opened A History of Warfare with “War is not the continuation of policy by other means,” calling war a cultural rather than a political activity; Christopher Bassford's reply is that Clausewitz's framework absorbs Keegan's point where Keegan's excludes his. [120]

otd.title: On this day · 8 November 1944
otd.body: On 8 November the withdrawal of the US 28th Infantry Division's 112th Infantry from Kommerscheidt was ordered, after six days of the battle for Schmidt that Germans call the Allerseelenschlacht; “am 8. November wurde schließlich der Rückzug befohlen”, on 8 November the withdrawal was finally ordered. [162] After dark the survivors came back down the Kall trail, which drops almost 500 feet into the gorge, towards Vossenack, while a German medical officer arranged local truces at the aid station by the Kall bridge to exchange wounded. The division had “sustained 6,184 casualties in just six days of fighting”, and Schmidt fell only on 7 February 1945. [163, 162] The ground is walked today as the Kall Trail, Rureifel route 66, 8.5 km, about 40 km from Heerlen.
